newsitem.title: GERMANY: German "Phoenix" channel takes aim at news TV.
newsitem.headline: German "Phoenix" channel takes aim at news TV.

text.p: Mixing raucous parliamentary debates, political documentaries with and coverage of breaking news, Germany's new Phoenix channel hopes to launch a new era of news broadcasting.
The new channel hits the airwaves on Monday and will kick off with a live broadcast of German President Roman Herzog receiving an honorary doctorate from the University of Tokyo.

Later in the week, Phoenix plans live broadcasts of rulings from the German Constitutional Court, a session of the European Parliament and a trade union conference in Berlin that is expected to debate Germany's record high unemployment.

These broadcasts may not exactly compete for big prime-time audiences but it is politics pure that is meant to inform those who really want to see news as it happens and further the national debate on key issues that affect the broad population.
"Phoenix is a new television offering that in this form cannot otherwise be found in Germany or anywhere else in Europe," said programme manager Barbara Groth.

The channel will introduce sign-language interpreters for the deaf during regular news broadcasts. In addition to domestic political debates, it wants to broadcast occasional live sessions of the Russian and British parliaments.

Designed to offer a blend of CNN-style breaking news coverage and the live, commentary-free broadcasts of parliamentary sessions modelled after the C-SPAN channel of the United States, Phoenix hopes to be a public service and appeal to news junkies in Germany.
But the station, a joint project of the ARD and ZDF public broadcasting networks, has had a rough start.
Dubbed the "events channel", the Phoenix launch was postponed for a week -- because there were no worthwhile events to broadcast.
The Easter holiday period is traditionally one of the slowest times of the year in Germany as politicians stay home.
Phoenix also has not yet been awarded full transmission rights in German cable TV networks.

If not for the unexpected opening last week of a slot on the Astra satellite network -- guaranteeing that at least six million German households could view the programme -- it would have been limited to networks in a handful of German cities.
By contrast, there are more than 16 million cable TV subscribers in Germany.
Klaus Radke, Phoenix's second programme director, said he expects the channel will be available to at least 80 percent of German TV viewers by the beginning of next year.
Phoenix is not alone with its problems gaining access to German cable TV networks.

There are currently some 30 channels available in the basic analogue cable network. But there are so many broadcasters that media regulators have to force some channels to share a slot and sometimes force some channels out to make room for others.
